text:
How to Spot an Unlicensed Bookmaker in a Few Easy Steps 🚩

A scam sportsbook rarely looks like one.
The site is slick. The bonus is huge. The odds look sharper than anywhere else. Signing up takes thirty seconds, and your deposit shows up in your account almost instantly. Everything feels smooth, until you try to withdraw.
Then the withdrawal is "pending." Then it's "under review." Then support asks for another document, and another, and another. Eventually the replies stop coming. Sometimes the site disappears altogether.
This happens to bettors every day, and the hardest part is what comes next. When a bookmaker has no licence, there's no regulator to call, no dispute service to step in, and nobody who can force them to pay. Your money is gone, and you have almost no way to get it back.
The good news is that unlicensed operators nearly always leave clues. If you know what to look for, you can spot most of them in a few minutes, before you deposit anything. Here's how:

Why a license matters
Before the warning signs, it helps to know what a license actually does for you, because it's much more than a logo in the footer.
A real gambling license legally requires an operator to:
• Keep player funds safe, often separate from the company's own operating money
• Pay out legitimate winnings
• Submit to independent dispute resolution when you have a complaint
• Offer responsible gambling tools such as deposit limits, time-outs and self-exclusion
• Follow rules on fair terms, advertising and identity checks
A licensed operator that breaks those rules can be fined, sanctioned or shut down. That threat is what keeps them honest.
An unlicensed operator owes you none of this. If they refuse to pay, your only "protection" is their goodwill, and goodwill doesn't process withdrawals.
So the most important question about any bookmaker isn't how big the bonus is or how good the odds are. It's who regulates it, and whether that regulator would actually do anything if the bookmaker didn't pay you.
---
Step 1: Verify the license. Don't just look at it 🔍
Every legitimate bookmaker shows its regulator, license number and registered company name, usually in the footer of the homepage.
But seeing a license isn't the same as checking it. Logos are easy to copy. Anyone can paste a regulator's badge onto a website, make up a license number, or borrow the details of a real company. Scam sites do this all the time because they know most people never check.
Here's how to check it yourself:
1️⃣ Find the regulator's official website on your own. Search for the regulator by name. Don't click the badge or link on the bookmaker's site, because a fake site can link to a fake "verification" page that looks real.
2️⃣ Use the regulator's public license register. Most reputable regulators publish a searchable list of licensed operators. Search for the company name, the brand name and the license number.
3️⃣ Check the details carefully. Confirm that:
• The license is currently active, not expired, suspended or revoked
• It covers sports betting, not just casino games or another product
• The company named on the register matches the company named on the site
• The exact domain you're on is listed under that license
That last point matters more than people expect. Scammers sometimes build clone sites that copy a real licensed brand's design and license details. The license is real, but it doesn't belong to the site you're on. If the domain isn't on the register, treat it as unlicensed.
🚩 Red flags:
• No license information anywhere on the site
• A regulator badge that isn't clickable, or that links somewhere unofficial
• A license number that doesn't appear on the regulator's register
• An expired, suspended or revoked license
• A company name that changes between the footer, the terms and the register
• A license that covers a different product or a different domain
If you can't verify the license in a few minutes, don't deposit. A legitimate operator makes this easy because it wants you to check.
---
Step 2: Inspect the site and the terms 🔒
Once you've checked the license, look at the site itself. Scam operators often move fast. They launch, collect deposits, shut down and reopen under a new name, and the rush tends to show.
Security
Look for the HTTPS padlock in your browser's address bar on every page, especially the sign-up, deposit and cashier pages. No padlock means walk away. Never enter card details or personal documents on an unsecured page. A padlock alone doesn't prove a site is honest, since scammers can get certificates too, but a missing one is an instant fail.
Quality
Persistent typos, broken links, missing pages, placeholder text, and "About Us" sections with no real information all suggest a site that was put together quickly. Pay close attention to the brand name and URL. Scammers love names that are almost identical to famous bookmakers: one letter swapped, an extra hyphen, a different domain ending. Read the URL letter by letter before you log in or deposit.
Bonus terms
This is where many scams hide in plain sight. A huge welcome bonus is the bait, and the terms are the trap. Watch for:
• Extreme wagering requirements of 50x or more, which make the bonus almost impossible to clear
• Maximum withdrawal caps that limit what you can cash out no matter how much you win
• Vague "irregular play" or "bonus abuse" clauses that let the operator void your winnings for almost any reason
• Terms that contradict the advertised offer
• Clauses giving the operator "sole discretion" to confiscate funds or close accounts without explanation
If an offer seems too good to be true, it usually is. Reputable bookmakers offer competitive promotions, but they don't need to promise the impossible to get your attention.
🚩 Red flags:
• A domain registered only weeks ago (you can check this with a public WHOIS lookup)
• No registered company name or physical address
• Terms and conditions copied from another site, sometimes with the other brand's name still in them
• Terms that change without notice, or that you can't find before signing up
---
Step 3: Check the banking 💸
How a bookmaker handles money tells you almost everything.
Scam operators are built to take money in fast and let it out slowly, or never. Deposits are instant and frictionless. Withdrawals are delayed, blocked, or wrapped in so many conditions that most people give up.
Before you deposit, read the payments page and the withdrawal terms. Look for:
• Clear processing times for withdrawals
• Reasonable minimum and maximum withdrawal limits
• Fees disclosed upfront, not discovered at cashout
• Familiar, traceable payment methods
• A clear explanation of the identity checks you'll go through, and when
Identity verification is normal, by the way. Licensed bookmakers are legally required to confirm who you are. The difference is that a legitimate operator tells you what it needs and processes it in a reasonable time. A scam operator uses "verification" as a stalling tactic, asking for one more document each time you request a payout.
🚩 Red flags:
• Crypto-only payments combined with no verifiable license
• Withdrawal minimums set absurdly high
• Surprise fees that only appear when you try to cash out
• Verification demands that escalate every time you request a withdrawal
• Pressure to deposit more before a withdrawal can be "unlocked"
• Withdrawals that get "reversed" back into your betting balance
✅ A smart test: deposit a small amount, place a modest bet, and request a withdrawal early, before you risk real money. If a small withdrawal comes through smoothly and on time, that's a good sign. If it stalls, gets reversed or comes with sudden new conditions, you've learned what you needed to know for the price of a small deposit.
---
Step 4: Research reputation and support 🗣️
Ignore the testimonials on the bookmaker's own website. They're written or chosen by the operator, and fake reviews cost nothing to produce.
Look for independent information instead:
• Independent betting forums and communities
• Third-party review sites
• Complaint platforms and dispute-resolution services
• News coverage and regulator warnings
A useful shortcut: search the brand name with words like "scam," "won't pay," "withdrawal problem" or "complaint." One unhappy customer doesn't prove much, because every business gets some complaints. What matters is the pattern. Lots of people describing the same withdrawal problem is a serious warning sign.
Also check whether the brand has a history under other names. Some operators shut down when complaints pile up, then relaunch with a new name, logo and domain, but the same terms, design and support scripts. If a brand seems to have appeared out of nowhere with no track record, be careful.
Then test customer support yourself before depositing. Ask simple, direct questions:
• "Which regulator licenses you, and what's your license number?"
• "How long do withdrawals usually take?"
• "Are there any fees or limits on withdrawals?"
A legitimate operator will answer clearly and consistently. A scam operator will dodge, give vague answers, contradict its own terms, or leave you with a bot that never hands you to a person.
🚩 Red flags:
• Lots of complaints about unpaid withdrawals
• Scripted five-star reviews that all sound the same
• A brand that disappeared and came back under a new name
• Bot-only support with no way to reach a person
• Support that won't answer licensing questions
• The operator appearing on a watchdog's or regulator's blacklist
---
Step 5: Watch for pressure tactics ⏳
Regulated operators have to follow strict advertising and marketing rules. They can't promise guaranteed wins, target vulnerable people, or pressure you into depositing more than you can afford.

quotedTweet.text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

🚨 Exposing a brand in India? 

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

text:
A friend of mine is being buried in paper.

His adversary keeps filing complaints against him with different authorities, one after another. Each complaint runs from 150 to 900 pages.

Every page sounds plausible. The allegations are structured, logical and full of references, and almost all of them are baseless.

That doesn't matter, though, because each one has to be answered.

Filing a complaint costs his adversary almost nothing. Answering it costs my friend lawyers, weeks of document collection, replies, hearings and appearances. Then the next complaint arrives at another authority, and it starts again.

His legal bills are enormous, and he hasn't done anything wrong.

This is the future of legal work in India, and most people are looking the wrong way.

There's an old idea called Brandolini's law: the effort needed to refute nonsense is an order of magnitude bigger than the effort needed to produce it.

AI has just made producing it nearly free.

A few years ago, a 900-page complaint needed a team and real money. Today, one angry person with a chatbot can produce it in an afternoon, polished, cited and convincing to anyone who doesn't check every line.

Generating allegations costs almost nothing. Refuting them is still expensive, and that asymmetry is going to reshape Indian legal practice.

Everyone keeps asking which legal jobs AI will kill. Routine drafting, contract review and friendly deals will shrink, because when both sides want the same standard outcome, AI gets there quickly.

But where one side wants to hurt the other, AI is a weapon, and weapons create work for the defence.

Here is where I think work will increase for Indian lawyers:

1. Defending against complaint warfare
Multi-forum complaints to police, regulators, tax authorities, professional bodies, consumer forums and RERA. Someone has to read, analyse and answer every one of them, and that work grows fastest.

2. Quashing and stopping abuse of process
Petitions under Section 528 BNSS (old 482 CrPC), writs against mechanical show-cause notices, and applications to club, stay or transfer proceedings across forums. Lawyers who can shut down a frivolous proceeding early will be worth their weight in gold.

3. Making the attacker pay
Exemplary costs, malicious prosecution suits, defamation actions and perjury applications against false statements. Today these remedies are underused. When complaints become cheap, raising the cost for the person filing them becomes the main defensive strategy.

4. Regulatory and show-cause defence
Departments will use AI too. Expect more notices, more data-matched queries and more automated demands. Every one of them needs a human answer that will hold up.

5. Corporate whistleblower and POSH complaints
Internal complaints will get longer, more frequent and more legalistic. Companies will need lawyers to run inquiries that are fast, fair and defensible.

6. Triage and rebuttal at scale
The winning firms won't answer 900 pages with 900 pages. They'll use AI to map every allegation, find the contradictions, match each claim to documents and draft responses fast, and then put human judgment on the 5 allegations that actually matter.

The lawyers who will do best in the next decade aren't the ones who write the most. They're the ones who can look at 900 pages of plausible nonsense and say, "Only these 3 points are real. Here's how we kill the rest, and here's how we make them pay for it."

AI makes complaining trivial. It makes defending expensive, and that's where the work is going.

If you're a young lawyer in India, don't just learn to draft. Learn to defend: procedure, forum strategy, quashing, costs and cross-examination.

And use AI to answer at the same speed it's being used against your clients.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
A Hyderabad founder spent four months building a B2B SaaS product. CRM integrations, three pricing tiers, onboarding that actually worked.

Two weeks before launch his co-founder asked what the cookie banner said.

There was no cookie banner. There were two documents, and neither of them had been written for this product.

The Terms of Service came from a competitor’s site. The Privacy Policy came from a template generator. Both had been pasted in during week one and never opened again.

He reached out to us with fourteen days on the clock. He was not asking for a document set. He wanted to know whether what he already had would survive contact with a paying customer.

So we read both documents against the product, not against each other.

The Privacy Policy said the platform collects name, email, and company name. That was true as far as it went.

It said nothing about the session replay tool running on every page, recording mouse movement and clicks from every visitor. 

Nothing about the analytics platform receiving behaviour data on export. 

Nothing about the CRM integration pulling contact records out of the customer’s own account.

Three tools were processing user data and a user reading the policy would never know they existed.

Under the DPDP Act, 2023 and the Rules notified on 13 November 2025, the notice has to itemize what is collected, the purpose, the retention, and who it is shared with. 

A policy that names three fields and omits three processors is not a short policy. It is an inaccurate one.

Then the liability cap. The template had a blank where the number goes and nobody had filled it in, so the contract capped his liability at zero.

Founders hear that and assume it is maximum protection. It is the opposite. 

A limitation clause that strips out all liability is the one most likely to be read against the drafter, and under UK law an unreasonable exclusion can be struck down entirely, which leaves the liability uncapped. 

The clause meant to protect him was the one most likely to disappear in a dispute.

The acceptable use clause prohibited uploading anything illegal. It said nothing about who owns uploaded data, whether the platform could use it to improve the product, or what happens to it when a subscription ends.

This is B2B. Every upload was a business customer’s data, which usually means it was someone else’s customer data two steps down the chain. Silence in the Terms is not a neutral position on that. If anything in the stack learns from customer data, silence means it is happening without a license.

The part I keep seeing is the sequence. 

Founders treat legal documents as a launch-day chore, something to generate the night before, when they are actually a product specification written in another language. 

The documents describe what the software does. If nobody checks them against what the software does, they describe a different product.

What I found harder to watch here was how well everything else had been built. 

Four months of careful work, and the one artefact he had outsourced to a template site was the first thing an enterprise buyer would open.

Here is what we did in the fourteen days.

We mapped every tool with access to user data, including the ones installed by his developer and never documented anywhere.

We rewrote the privacy notice to cover all of them, with purpose, retention, and third-party sharing set out against each.

We put a defensible number in the liability cap and rebuilt the clause around it.

We drafted the data ownership, permitted use, and model training position, plus deletion and export on termination.

We added the IT Rules disclosures, legal entity details and a named grievance officer, to the footer and the Terms.

The product launched three weeks later with a complete set. One week after that, the first enterprise prospect asked for a security and compliance review before signing. He had answers.

The comparison is not close. Two weeks of drafting before launch, against a DPDP penalty regime that runs up to ₹250 crore for security safeguard failures, and against the thing that actually kills early deals, which is a procurement team deciding you are too much work to onboard.

So here are three things to check before your next customer invite goes out.

Open your Privacy Policy and list every tool on your site that touches user data. Analytics, session replay, chat widget, CRM, email platform. If an SDK is installed and not named, your notice is wrong. Naming the obvious ones and skipping the rest is not a shorter policy.

Find the number in your liability cap. If the clause is blank, inherited, or set to zero, that is not conservative drafting. It is the clause your buyer’s counsel will spend the most time on.

Read what your Terms say about uploaded data. Ownership, permitted use, what happens on termination, and whether anything in your stack improves on it. If the document is silent on all four, you are relying on an assumption you never wrote down.

Two dates are now fixed. The Consent Manager framework switches on 13 November 2026. The obligations on notice, consent, security, and data principal rights apply from 13 May 2027.

Most founders who send us their documents believe the legal side is handled because the pages exist. 

The pages existing and the pages matching the product are different things, and the buyer’s counsel is the one who checks.

GST return filed late with interest and late fee after Best Judgment Assessment: Andhra Pradesh High Court holds assessment order stands "deemed to have been withdrawn".

Issue:
Whether an ex-parte best judgment assessment order passed under Section 62 of the CGST/APGST Act, 2017 stands "deemed to have been withdrawn" when the Assessee furnishes the overdue return beyond the statutory period along with full tax, applicable interest, and late fee.

Rule:
Under Section 62(1) of the CGST/APGST Act, 2017, where a registered person fails to furnish returns under Section 39, the proper officer may assess tax liability on a best-judgment basis. Section 62(2) provides that where the Assessee subsequently furnishes a valid return within the prescribed statutory period from service of the assessment order, the assessment order is "deemed to have been withdrawn", while retaining liability for interest under Section 50(1) and late fee under Section 47. Judicial precedent extends this benefit where statutory dues, interest, and late fees stand fully discharged.

Application:
The Assessee failed to file its monthly GSTR-3B return for January 2023 within the statutory deadline under Section 39. Consequently, the Department issued a best judgment assessment order dated 17.04.2023 under Section 62, raising a tax demand of Rs. 12,61,060 along with interest. Subsequently, the Assessee submitted its GSTR-1 on 11.05.2023 and GSTR-3B on 29.05.2023, while depositing the entire tax liability, applicable interest, and late fee. Since the primary objective of Section 62 is to secure statutory compliance and revenue rather than sustain arbitrary demands, the belated filing accompanied by statutory interest and late fee cures the default. Because the Assessee fully remitted the tax dues together with late fees and interest, the beneficial mandate of Section 62(2) squarely applies, following the rule settled in Brothers Engineering and Errectors Ltd. and Helmet House.

Conclusion:
Because the Assessee complied by filing the requisite return and tendering the tax, interest, and late fees, the High Court held that the best judgment assessment order dated 17.04.2023 stands deemed to have been withdrawn under Section 62(2), barring the Department from initiating or continuing any recovery proceedings against the Assessee.

Impact Analysis:
This ruling provides substantial relief to taxpayers facing Section 62 best-judgment orders by affirming that belatedly filing the return along with tax, interest, and late fees nullifies the departmental assessment and prevents coercive recovery.

Department drags Assessee into time-barred demands and parallel ITC proceedings; High Court steps in to quash the demand order.

Issue :
The primary controversy was whether the Demand-cum-Show Cause Notice issued under Section 74(1) for the financial year 2017-18 was hopelessly barred by the statutory period of limitation prescribed under Section 74(10) of the CGST Act. The companion controversy was whether central tax authorities retained jurisdiction to initiate proceedings concerning excess Input Tax Credit for the financial years 2018-19 and 2019-20 when state tax authorities had already initiated and dropped proceedings on the identical subject matter, attracting the statutory bar under Section 6(2)(b) of the CGST Act.

Rule:
Section 74(10) of the CGST Act mandates that any adjudication order must be passed within a strict outer limit of five years from the statutory due date for furnishing the annual return, and administrative extensions granting taxpayers extra time to file returns do not automatically stretch the Department's period of limitation. Under Section 6(2)(b) of the CGST Act, as settled by the Supreme Court in M/s Armour Security (India) Ltd., where one tax administration has formally commenced adjudicatory proceedings by issuing a show cause notice on a specific tax liability, the other tax administration is strictly prohibited from initiating parallel proceedings on the same subject matter. Furthermore, the exceptional five-year window under Section 74(1) strictly requires explicit jurisdictional preconditions of fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression of facts to evade tax, none of which can be assumed from routine investigative scrutiny or audit letters.

Application:
Regarding the financial year 2017-18, the statutory due date for filing the annual return was 31.12.2018, which meant the five-year limitation period available to the Department conclusively expired on 31.12.2023. The Department issued the impugned show cause notice only on 22.07.2024. Notification No. 06/2020 issued under Section 168A was purely intended to mitigate taxpayer hardship by extending return-filing dates and did not enlarge the Department's statutory limitation to initiate recovery. Moreover, an earlier inquiry letter dated 22.03.2021 was merely an administrative probe regarding VAT deposits rather than an adjudicatory notice alleging fraud or suppression. Regarding the financial years 2018-19 and 2019-20, state authorities had already issued show cause notices for mismatches between credit ledger entries and annual returns before dropping those proceedings. The central authority’s subsequent notice covering the identical excess credit issue violated Section 6(2)(b) because it sought to re-adjudicate an identical infraction. Conversely, allegations regarding short payment of tax for those years and return mismatches for the financial year 2020-21 were distinct causes of action and remained legally permissible.

Conclusion:
The High Court held that the proceedings for the financial year 2017-18 were completely barred by limitation and that the proceedings concerning excess Input Tax Credit for the financial years 2018-19 and 2019-20 were hit by the bar against parallel proceedings under Section 6(2)(b). Consequently, the High Court partly quashed the show cause notice to the extent of these jurisdictional defects, set aside the Order-in-Original in its entirety, and remitted the matter back to the Joint Commissioner for fresh adjudication strictly confined to the surviving issues within three months, reserving full liberty to the Assessee to contest the invocation of Section 74 on merits.

Impact Analysis:
This ruling protects taxpayers from dual scrutiny by preventing Centre and State authorities from reopening identical credit mismatches while making it clear that the Department cannot stretch statutory limitation periods using routine return-filing extension notifications.

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Can the Government suspend a political party’s Instagram handle without a clear statutory power? And can a politician boycott a courtroom while simultaneously asking the Supreme Court to transfer the same judge from hearing his case?  

This week, the Aam Aadmi Party raised both questions in two different constitutional courtrooms.  

In the Supreme Court, AAP challenged the suspension of its Gujarat unit’s Instagram handle, arguing that Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act was never meant to become a direct content-blocking weapon. 

Senior Advocate Shadan Farasat argued that the provision only deals with “safe harbour” obligations of intermediaries — not independent censorship powers.  The party says the move violates Article 19(1)(a), the constitutional guarantee of free speech. 

The Supreme Court has now issued notice to the Centre.  At the same time in the Delhi High Court, Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma appointed three amicus curiae for Arvind Kejriwal, Manish Sisodia, and Satyendar Jain after the leaders chose to boycott proceedings, invoking “Mahatma Gandhi’s Satyagraha principles” and claiming their faith in the court process had been shaken.  

But here’s the constitutional twist: Kejriwal had also moved the Supreme Court seeking transfer of the excise policy case away from Justice Sharma’s bench — even as his legal team withdrew from participation before her court.  

This has now created a rare constitutional confrontation involving: 
⚖️ Article 19 vs state regulation of digital speech 
⚖️ Article 21 vs procedural fairness in criminal prosecution 
⚖️ Judicial recusal vs courtroom boycott 
⚖️ Free speech, due process, and strategic constitutional litigation  Justice Sharma’s response may become one of the most significant procedural moments in the case: instead of proceeding ex parte, she chose to appoint independent senior advocates as amicus curiae to preserve procedural fairness.  

And one line from the Supreme Court hearing may define this entire battle: “Today my portal is gone.”  Because this is no longer just about an Instagram account.

 It is about whether opposition parties in India can lose their digital voice overnight — and what constitutional remedy exists when that happens.

"How the Supreme Court’s trans ruling is paving the way for a return of gender-neutral loos

The ruling could see a renewed push for unisex lavatories – but critics say the facilities may create safeguarding risks

As businesses and organisations grapple with the implications of last week’s Supreme Court ruling on “sex” meaning “biological sex”, one particular issue appears – once again – to be at the forefront of the gender debate: lavatories.

Which facilities should men who identify as women now use? What about trans men (women who identify as men)? Or even those who identify as non-binary?

Coincidentally, on Wednesday, a judge in Scotland ordered that Scottish schools should provide single-sex toilets, in response to a claim brought against Scottish Borders Council (SBC). The local authority had installed gender-neutral toilets at a primary school, to the chagrin of parents who believed that boys and girls should have access to separate loos.

But campaigners fear that last week’s Supreme Court ruling, which led to the Government saying that trans women should use toilets according to their biological sex, will simply lead to a renewed push for gender-neutral or unisex lavatories, which have also proved highly divisive. Those facilities sometimes involve women sharing with men using urinals, or rows of cubicles used by both sexes.

“What trans person will now use a public lavatory without fear of abuse, or worse?” said Sir Stephen Wall, a former senior civil servant and LGBT activist. “If the Government is serious about human rights, it should mandate the provision of gender-neutral facilities wherever separate provision is at present made for men and women.”

Baroness Falkner of Margravine, who chairs the UK’s Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) has said that the ruling brought clarity and that facilities “must be based on biological sex”. But she suggested that many organisations may need to provide a “third space” for trans customers or employees.

Nightclubs in the late 1990s were the first to experiment with gender-neutral toilets Credit: Charday Penn

“There isn’t any law saying you cannot use a neutral third space and they should be using their powers of advocacy to ask for those third spaces.”

Only last year, the Conservative government’s changes to building regulations meant that new restaurants, shopping centres, offices and public toilets would have to feature separate single-sex lavatories for women and men. The new legislation followed government consultation which found that 81 per cent of people “agreed with the intention for separate single-sex toilet facilities.”

Now it appears that last week’s Supreme Court judgment might lead to the return of gender neutral loos – if only as an additional, “third” space, and quite possibly at considerable expense to the companies responsible for each building. Last week, it emerged that one council had spent £13,400 making one public lavatory block gender neutral, in 2021.

Public lavatories have been available in Britain since around the mid-19th century but initially only for men. Victorian women had to campaign to be unshackled from the “urinary leash” which meant they could only go so far before needing to return home to relieve themselves.

Female-only toilets started to emerge in the first half of the 20th century, with Selfridges being the first department store to offer public toilets for women when it opened in 1909.

But unisex toilets are a relatively recent invention, with nightclubs in the late 1990s being the first to experiment.

By the early 2000s, schools were beginning to introduce these unisex bathrooms. One of the first was Bramhall High School in Stockport, near Manchester, in 2000.

John Peckham, the head teacher at the time, suggested that the unisex cubicles opening into a shared washbasin area would prevent bullying, vandalism and smoking. But even then, parents expressed concerns that their child might be embarrassed using them or it would encourage sexual liaisons between the pupils.

The Department of Education (DfE) was also not in favour, stating that “the time is not right for the introduction of unisex toilets in our schools”. Yet just seven years later, it issued new guidance encouraging all new schools in England to fit unisex toilets.

Should organisations replace single-sex toilets with unisex spaces?

Yes

No

Discuss in the comments

Total votes: 73

In January 2009, University of Staffordshire started trialling gender-neutral toilets in its nightclub. “We do have transgender students here, but the new facilities are not just for them – they are for the androgynous students as well,” said Fee Wood, the student union president at the time.

Over the next decade, more unisex toilets would be fitted into academic institutions such as Lancaster, Leeds and Sheffield Universities.

But protests continued. In 2014, parents complained after Harbour Primary and Nursery School in Newhaven, East Sussex introduced unisex lavatories at the start of the school year.

Three years later, the headmaster of the £26,000-a-year Highgate School in North London, which had installed the toilets, issued an apology to parents saying: “I’m aware this change has left a number of pupils, particularly Years 7 and 8 feeling less comfortable and happy at school.”

Tracy Shaw, of Safe Schools Alliance UK, which campaigns to uphold safeguarding in schools says that unisex toilets in schools create safeguarding risks.

“Organisations are saying they need time to reflect on the Supreme Court ruling and review their policies but in the case of schools they should not need to,” she says. “Regardless of what it said in the Equality Act, schools should have been reviewing all guidance from a safeguarding point of view and resisting changes that put children at risk.

“Girls’s toilets are for girls. Gender neutral toilets that have no gap under the door are not as safe as toilets that do not have to be completely closed off to prevent voyeurism, because the lack of a gap means that collapse, self-harm or assault goes undetected. This is a safeguarding issue.”

Maya Forstater, chief executive of the Sex Matters campaign group, says, ‘It is absolutely fine to have single-user unisex options alongside dedicated male and female toilets’ Credit: Iain Masterton/Alamy Stock Photo

The gender-neutral trend was not confined to academia. It also swept through Whitehall with the Home Office changing its ten single-sex toilets in 2018 to unisex at a cost of £40,000. Some female members of staff were so unhappy they began walking to the Ministry of Communities, Housing and Local Government to use the female toilets there.

Reportedly, a note was pinned to one of the Home Office’s new toilets which read: “Polite notice: Could men using these toilets please use them with the door shut. Women are finding the use of these toilets quite distressing.”

Venues such as the Barbican Centre and The Old Vic also followed suit. While some welcomed the change, again there was backlash.

In January 2022, a YouGov poll echoed the feelings of those who had publicly opposed the changes. It showed that 87 per cent of people wanted separate toilets for men and women with 35 per cent also supporting the idea of a unisex toilet. Only seven per cent of people wanted a unisex toilet option exclusively.

Heather Binning, director of the Women’s Rights Network, says the campaign group supports the idea of unisex facilities – but not at the expense of women and girls.

“We have fought long and hard over recent years for the rights for women and girls and a specific battle has been the right to have female-only toilets,” she says. “We are the sex that copes with menstruation and pregnancy, and various problems associated with both.

These actions often happen under two parallel mechanisms of India’s Information Technology Act, 2000.

First, under Section 69A, which allows the government to issue blocking orders on broad grounds such as national security or public order. Read with Rule 16 of the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009, this provision requires confidentiality regarding all requests and complaints received, as well as actions taken.

Second, Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, 2000, allows authorities to pressure platforms to remove content by threatening loss of “safe harbour” protections if platforms fail to comply with government or court directions. In practice, this creates strong incentives for platforms to over-comply.

Since this story started trending, I have seen different versions of what happened...

Some people say the couple had s€xual intercourse inside a mosque in Makkah...Others say they only kissed... Some have even shared pictures claiming to show their execution.

I had to go search because online rumours sometimes are worris0me.

So, what exactly happened?

On Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Saudi Arabia announced the execution of two Bangladeshi nationals, a man and a woman, in the Makkah region.

According to Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Interior, the two had been arrested following an investigation and taken through legal proceedings... The court found them guilty of what the authorities described as an “immoral act” inside a mosque.

The court sentenced them to death under ta'zir, a category of discretionary punishment under Islamic law...

 According to the Saudi statement, the severity of the offence and the violation of the sanctity of the time and place were considered...The verdict was upheld and a royal order was issued for the executions.

But here is where the story becomes more complicated.

What exactly did the couple do inside the mosque?

The Saudi authorities did not publicly explain the precise act in their announcement... They did not identify the mosque or provide detailed information about the circumstances of the incident.

This is why different versions began circulating online, with some people claiming that the couple had s€x while others said they had only kissed.

However, subsequent reporting by The Daily Star in Bangladesh stated that a message from the Bangladesh mission's Labour Welfare Wing described the allegation as adultery inside a mosque.

So, while adultery was reported as the allegation, the full details of the incident have not been made public in the reports available.

And what did Bangladesh say?

Bangladesh said its diplomatic mission had not been informed before the executions took place.

After learning of the matter, the Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah sought clarification from Saudi authorities. 

On 18 October, Bangladesh's Ministry of Foreign Affairs also sought an explanation from the Saudi ambassador.

By 19 October, Bangladesh was still seeking further information about the case.

Another report revealed that the two individuals' names had appeared on a list of prisoners previously shared with the Bangladeshi mission, but the list did not disclose that they had received death sentences.

A picture/video being shared as footage of this particular execution was fact-checked and found to be from an unrelated incident in 2015. 

It was not footage of the two Bangladeshis executed in October 2026.

This is another reminder that a video can be real while the story attached to it is false.

That is what I found....

Now, I am sharing this not to judge the couple, condemn Saudi Arabia, defend anybody or encourage anyone to disrespect the sanctity of a mosque.

I simply want us to separate what has been confirmed from what people are assuming.

We know that the executions were announced. 

We know what the Saudi authorities said about the conviction... We know that Bangladesh sought an explanation after learning of the executions.

But the precise details of what happened inside that mosque have not been fully established in the public reports available to anyone...

As Muslims, we can recognise the sanctity of the holy places while also being careful about what we say concerning people's lives, deaths and legal cases.

We do not have to invent details to make a story powerful... We do not have to take sides before understanding the facts.

Sometimes, the most responsible thing to say is simply, This is what we know, this is what has been reported and this is what we still do not know... 

People can talk down on your religion without any tangible/reasonable fact- check... Let them... It doesn't start today, so it won't end now...

Section 43(1) of the DPDP Act lets the central government make an order, published in the Gazette, to remove a difficulty in giving effect to the Act. The order must not be inconsistent with the Act.

Section 43(2) bars any such order after three years from the date the Act comes into force, and section 43(3) requires every order to be laid before each House of Parliament as soon as it is made. This video is said to be from 2009. Look at how the Election Commission of India functioned then, and compare it with what is happening today.

The Election Commission freely encouraged citizens to exercise their voting rights. Its advertisements highlighted the problems people faced in everyday life, including corruption, poor education, inadequate healthcare, crumbling infrastructure and bad governance, and reminded them that the power to change these conditions lay in their votes.

The central purpose was to promote universal adult franchise, encourage electoral participation and increase voter turnout.

Watch this advertisement carefully. It clearly conveys the message that if the government has failed to deliver good governance, the citizens have the power to change it through elections.

Did anyone accuse the Election Commission of being biased or campaigning against the government? Did the government have to rush to its defence? Or was the Election Commission simply exercising its constitutional independence?

In 2013, following the Supreme Court’s intervention, VVPAT was introduced to strengthen transparency and build confidence among voters and political parties. The Supreme Court recognised that an independently verifiable paper trail was indispensable to free and fair elections.

Now look at what is happening.

When questions were raised about the extraordinary increase in reported voter turnout after 5 PM, political parties and citizens sought access to CCTV footage and election records.

The Punjab and Haryana High Court directed the Election Commission to provide the relevant footage and records. What followed?

Instead of making election records more accessible, the Central Government amended Rule 93 of the Conduct of Election Rules in December 2024, on the Election Commission’s recommendation, restricting public access to CCTV footage and other electronic election records.

Subsequently, the Election Commission introduced instructions permitting the destruction of CCTV footage and other recordings after just 45 days where no election petition had been filed.

Why should evidence relating to the conduct of elections be made inaccessible and then destroyed when transparency is precisely what establishes public confidence?

The Supreme Court rejected the demand for 100% VVPAT verification in 2024. But what is the purpose of an independently verifiable paper trail if its comprehensive verification is resisted? The very purpose of introducing VVPAT was to strengthen public confidence in election results.

And now we are witnessing something even more disturbing.

Instead of concentrating on enrolling every eligible citizen, the electoral roll revision has resulted in the removal of approximately 13 crore names. Genuine voters are being forced to struggle to establish their eligibility and recover their voting rights.

With an adult population exceeding 100 crore, the Election Commission must explain how many eligible citizens remain outside the electoral rolls and how many have been wrongly excluded.

The Election Commission’s constitutional responsibility is to ensure that every eligible citizen can vote, not to make citizens struggle to protect their existing voting rights.

Look at the complete reversal.

Earlier, the Election Commission encouraged citizens to vote, expanded participation and introduced measures to strengthen public confidence.
